headline: Quebec's SQDC lifts quarterly cannabis sales 10%; BC wholesale up 1%
dek: Quebec's state cannabis retailer sold C$207.5M in its fiscal second quarter as vapes and new stores lifted sales, while BC wholesale grew 1% to C$156.4M.
key_points: The SQDC reported C$207.5 million in sales and C$37.2 million in comprehensive income for the quarter ended 12 September, up from C$30.5 million in income a year earlier.
Non-flower products, helped by vapes the SQDC launched in November 2025, rose 41% to C$56.4 million, while dried flower edged up 1%.
BC's government wholesaler sold C$156.4 million of cannabis in the quarter to 30 September, up 1% in dollars and 3% in grams, as the average price slipped to C$3.70 a gram.
Together the two provinces show Canada's mature market growing on new formats and store counts, not on flower or price.
body: Two of Canada's provincial cannabis agencies reported second-quarter numbers this week, and both point the same way: growth is coming from new product formats and more stores, while dried flower stands still. Quebec's Société québécoise du cannabis (SQDC), the province's state-owned retail monopoly, posted C$207.5 million in sales for its second fiscal quarter, up 10% from a year earlier, StratCann reported on 12 November. British Columbia's government wholesaler sold C$156.4 million of cannabis in the quarter to 30 September, up just 1%, StratCann reported on 13 November.

The SQDC said the quarter, which ended on 12 September, produced comprehensive income of C$37.2 million, compared with C$30.5 million a year earlier. On top of that, it estimated C$77.8 million in consumer and excise taxes from its operations, with C$55.7 million going to Quebec and C$22.1 million to Ottawa.

Quebec sold 42,028 kilograms of cannabis in the quarter, up 8%, according to StratCann's account of the results. The SQDC credited six stores opened since the same quarter last year, longer opening hours at some branches and the vape products it launched in November 2025. The effect shows clearly in the product split: dried flower sales rose 1% to C$151.1 million, while all other products jumped 41% to C$56.4 million.

Flower still makes up about 73% of Quebec's sales, by MetaFlora's calculation, but the other 27% is where nearly all the growth is. Store sales reached C$199.4 million and online sales C$8.1 million, each up about 10% and 8%. The agency recorded 5.2 million transactions, up from 4.8 million, which works out to an average basket of about C$40. The average price including taxes rose slightly, to C$5.61 a gram from C$5.55.

With 114 stores at the end of the quarter, the SQDC averaged about C$1.8 million in sales per store over the 12-week period. It said it will keep refreshing branches and will reassess areas of the province that still lack a store. An SQDC commercial strategy manager told StratCann this autumn that the agency wants a balanced portfolio of suppliers from across Canada, not only Quebec producers.
> Canada's legal market is no longer growing on flower. It is growing on vapes, pre-rolls and store count.
## British Columbia: more grams, lower prices

BC's numbers come from the provincial Liquor Distribution Branch's wholesale arm, which supplies private stores. Its C$156.4 million covered 42.25 million grams, StratCann reported, so volume grew faster than dollars for the second quarter in a row. The average wholesale price across all products fell 5 cents from a year earlier to C$3.70 a gram, and dried flower fell a cent to C$3.12.

The product mix tells the same story as Quebec. Grams of dried flower sold fell 5% and flower sales in dollars fell 6%. Pre-roll units rose 7% and their dollar sales 8%; inhalable extracts, which include vapes, infused pre-rolls and hash, rose 3% to C$58.8 million. Infused pre-rolls were 36% of that category and disposable vape units jumped 45%. Edible units fell 35% while edible dollar sales rose 2%, which StratCann linked to larger multipacks. BC's licensed store count rose 3% to 536, with all of the increase in the Lower Mainland.

BC's direct delivery program, which lets small producers sell straight to stores, grew faster from a smaller base: sales rose 42% to C$4.4 million, and at C$4.36 a gram its average price is well above the main wholesale channel.

BC has collected C$617.9 million as its share of federal cannabis excise duty through June 2026, the latest figures, including C$70.4 million in the first half of this year, StratCann reported. The province exported 61,184 kilograms of cannabis in the first nine months of 2026. Note that BC's figures are wholesale and Quebec's are retail including taxes, so the price per gram in the two provinces is not directly comparable.

For producers, the message from both agencies is that the shelf is being won in formats rather than in price per gram of flower. That favours companies with strong vape, pre-roll and extract lines, and makes a provincial listing in Quebec, where the SQDC alone decides what is stocked, especially valuable.

The federal excise stamp changes in Budget 2026, which we covered on 7 November, would cut the number of unique excise stamps from 13 and add enforcement tools; watch how quickly they reach the stores. The SQDC's third-quarter results, covering the holiday season, should follow in February if it keeps last year's timing. In BC, watch whether store growth outside the Lower Mainland resumes, and whether the province's 1 km separation debate, the subject of an ABLE BC webinar on 26 November, leads to a rule change. Statistics Canada's monthly retail figures will show whether the vape-led growth in Quebec and BC holds nationally.
